source.title: Interactions Between Crosscoder Features: A Compact Proofs Perspective
source.authors: Dmitry Manning-Coe; Thomas Read; Anna Soligo; Oliver Clive-Griffin; C. Yip; Rajashree Agrawal; Jason Gross

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse dictionary-feature analysis to TinyStories-Instruct-33M, an LLM setting, and evaluates whether crosscoder features have interpretable activation patterns. It does not reproduce the toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The feature-explanation validation results bear on V4. The interaction-penalty training and ablation results are induced by the study's training intervention; they do not establish that superposition or computational sparsity arises without that intervention. The feature-cluster accuracy result evaluates grouping, not whether the dictionary recovers the model's underlying features.
record.test_reason: The study uses acausal BatchTopK crosscoders as a tool. It derives an MLP feature-interaction metric from a compact-proof error term and uses it as a training penalty, for clustering, and for sleeper-agent anomaly detection. The GPT-4o sensitivity/specificity check (Sec. 4.3, Table 8) asks whether the authors' penalty harms interpretability; it has no neuron or random baseline. No result tests whether superposition exists, whether features are sparse and recoverable (V4), or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only the interpretability check. The main conclusions are these. A compact-proof error term yields an MLP feature-interaction metric. Penalizing it gives 'computationally sparse' crosscoders: 60% of MLP performance is retained with only the dominant feature per neuron and datapoint, versus 10% for standard crosscoders. The cost is modest reconstruction loss, similar across Pythia and TinyStories sizes, and interpretability is unchanged. Interaction-based clusters are semantically meaningful (66% judge accuracy), and sleeper-agent trigger tokens are more interacting. The authors note the bounds are vacuous for full models and that the experiments use small models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses acausal sparse crosscoders and an MLP feature-interaction metric rather than toy networks designed to study superposition; it does not sweep feature sparsity or assess near-orthogonal feature geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-explanation sensitivity and specificity are reported separately for λ=0 and λ=1000; the authors describe the results as extremely similar.

fits_no_version.finding: In standard crosscoders on TinyStories-Instruct-33M, the dominant crosscoder feature carries only ~30% of a neuron's L1 input norm on average. Keeping only the dominant feature retains ~10% of loss recovered, versus 63% at λ=200.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual MLP neurons receive substantial, computationally relevant contributions from several dictionary features at once (feature interaction at neurons).

fits_no_version.finding: In a one-layer modular-addition transformer, the penalty cannot concentrate more than ~60% of a neuron's norm on one feature without reconstruction breaking down. The authors attribute this to each neuron hosting sine and cosine components (App. F, Fig. 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How far computation can be concentrated onto one dictionary feature per neuron depends on the model; some models require multi-feature neurons.

record.problems: The feature-interpretability validation uses GPT-4o as judge. The authors state that they studied relatively small models and that whether the documented trade-offs carry over to frontier-like models remains unknown.
record.rows_left_out: Interaction-penalty sweeps, ablations, feature clustering, and sleeper-agent interaction results were not extracted as claim-version rows: they do not test the versions' claims about naturally arising superposition geometry or feature recovery.

untested.parts: No toy model, sparsity sweep, or feature geometry.
No test of capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of other causes of polysemantic neurons.
No baseline-controlled test that LLMs contain sparse dictionary-recoverable features or spread features across neurons.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity of dictionary features.
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4. The only extracted rows compare the authors' penalized crosscoder with the standard one on auto-interp scores, with no baseline (no neuron or random-direction comparison). They cannot show that the model contains recoverable sparse features, so no V4 verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-model feature-count, sparsity, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition test.
Does not test whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate other causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests crosscoder features in TinyStories-Instruct-33M, not SAE recovery or feature distribution across neurons; does not test larger or frontier models.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: TinyStories-Instruct-33M crosscoder features, with and without the interaction penalty
reader_labels.reason: GPT-4o validation gives high mean sensitivity and specificity for feature explanations in both conditions (R1–R4), supporting the limited finding that a sparse crosscoder can recover interpretable features in this model.
